criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design. Discusses context of ethical issues in engineering organisations. Identifies the relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Ethical issues (harm to end-users, professional responsibility, quality versus business pressure) and stakeholders are identified and linked to the case. Industry context is only briefly sketched, and the link to specific engineering design practice is thin. Stakeholder interests are named but not explored in the introduction, so this sits at Very good rather than Excellent.

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions of the ethical issues. Draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments for and against are presented with reasonable development, and a clear conclusion is reached. Depth is uneven: the for-side relies on opinion (e.g., 'may well be enough'), and recommendations target Rachel and her company, with the health department and chip contract company largely absent from the decision guidance.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument, which justifies the conclusion. The body of the report follows a logical structure, with paragraphs linked and content ordered in a way that is easy to follow and support the building of the argument. Arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The structure (for, against, ethical path, conclusion, recommendations) is easy to follow and the conclusion is supported by the harm and EACE arguments. The 'for' arguments are not systematically rebutted, and the analysis of all stakeholders is uneven, so it falls short of a systematic treatment for all stakeholders.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence. Research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Four references are used, with relevant case studies (NHS, Volkswagen) and the EACE. However, the Apple/Samsung/Google claim is weakly supported by a CNBC piece on marketing psychology, and most for-arguments lack external evidence. Quantitative evidence is absent, so research is moderate rather than in-depth.

technical_issues.where: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
technical_issues.issue: The claim that Apple outpaces Samsung and Google is unsupported by the cited CNBC article, which concerns marketing psychology rather than competitive advantage.
The NHS IT failures (data loss) are equated with Rachel's physical-harm hardware defects, and deaths are attributed causally without showing the link.

technical_issues.where: DICUSSION: To Ship or Not to Ship
technical_issues.issue: The scenario's decision threshold (no shipping for physical harm, shipping for data-loss) is not analysed, so how Rachel should determine when to ship is unanswered.
Reference formatting is inconsistent and incomplete: [3] lacks an author and URL, and [4] is garbled.

overall: A coherent, mostly well-argued report with a clear recommendation and relevant EACE and NHS/Volkswagen cases. Weaknesses are thin evidence for the for-arguments, no treatment of Rachel's decision threshold, uneven stakeholder analysis, several language and referencing errors, and no visual elements.

feedback.summary: You have written a coherent, well-structured report with a clear recommendation not to ship, supported by relevant NHS and Volkswagen cases and the EACE. Your strongest areas are your identification of harm to end-users and the logical flow from arguments to conclusion. The main areas to strengthen are the evidence behind the arguments for shipping, analysis of the decision threshold, referencing accuracy and language precision.
next_steps: Analyse the decision threshold in the scenario: explain when shipping might be acceptable (data-loss issues) versus when it is not (physical harm), and how Rachel should decide between them.

Strengthen the arguments for shipping with reputable external evidence and rebut them directly. Also show clearly how the NHS data-loss cases link to Rachel's physical-harm defects, rather than assuming the link.

Format all references consistently and completely (including authors and URLs for [3] and a corrected [4]), correct the language errors, and add at least one figure or table to support your discussion.

criteria.C1: You identify key ethical issues, including harm to end-users, professional responsibility and quality versus business pressure, and you name the main stakeholders in your introduction. To reach Excellent, briefly explore the industry context, link the issues more explicitly to specific engineering design practice, and develop each stakeholder's interests rather than only naming them.
criteria.C2: You present arguments for and against shipping and reach a clear conclusion. To move up, give the arguments for shipping more depth by supporting them with evidence rather than opinion, and rebut them directly. Extend your recommendations beyond Rachel and her company to include the health department and the chip contract company.
criteria.C3: Your report follows a logical sequence (for, against, ethical path, conclusion, recommendations), which makes the argument easy to follow and supports your conclusion on harm and professional integrity. To reach Excellent, systematically rebut the arguments for shipping and give all stakeholders an equally thorough analysis.
criteria.C4: You use four references, including relevant case studies and the EACE, to support your points. Some claims are weakly supported: the Apple/Samsung/Google claim is not backed by the CNBC source you cite, and most arguments for shipping lack external evidence. Add quantitative evidence and make sure each source supports the specific claim it is attached to.
criteria.C5: Your report includes the required sections and is generally readable. Correct the language errors, including the broken sentences, and check your word choice. Reference [3] needs an author and URL, and reference [4] needs reformatting. Adding figures or tables would strengthen your visual support.
